topic.title: The invite list is a blame list
topic.claim: A meeting with eleven people on the invite was never called to decide something; it was called so nobody has to decide alone.
topic.moment: A calendar invite titled 'Quick sync' with half the floor on it and no agenda.

turn.believed: Big meetings happen because many people need to give input.
turn.actually: Each extra name spreads the risk if the decision goes wrong.

topic.feeling: My whole day went into rooms where nothing happened.
topic.villain: Org structures that punish wrong calls more than slow ones
topic.because: When a decision can go wrong, the safest move is to have everyone in the room. Then the mistake belongs to nobody.
topic.payoff: The number of people in a meeting tells you how scared the organiser is.
topic.behaviour: Teams add stakeholders to every call and end with 'let's take this offline'.
topic.mechanism: Shared decisions mean shared blame, which means no blame.
topic.send_to: The colleague with back-to-back meetings and nothing done
topic.why_now: Calendars are full of planning meetings before the new financial year.

reader.point: Big meetings with too many invitees happen because people want to share the blame for decisions, not because they need discussion, and the real work gets pushed to later.
reader.reason: Making a decision alone puts your name on a possible mistake, while a slow group meeting spreads the blame across everyone, so people choose the meeting.

sources.fact: SHRM India says that when responsibility is shared without a single owner, individuals take less ownership and nobody is answerable for the outcome.
sources.stance: supports: This backs the idea that spreading a decision across many people leaves no one accountable. It does not say people add attendees on purpose to avoid blame, and it does not discuss committees.
sources.excerpt: shared responsibility, without clear individual ownership, routinely produces the opposite of what leaders intend. | When Everyone Owns a Responsibility, No One is Accountable | Ambiguity does not disappear when responsibility is shared. | Name one owner per outcome, even on shared initiatives. | only one person should be held accountable for its outcome. | Make accountability explicit in team meetings as a routine operating norm.

sources.fact: A Jabra study reports that Indian workers average 8.8 hours of meetings a week, most leave without clear action items, and many need follow-up meetings to clarify decisions.
sources.stance: neutral: The data shows meetings often end without decisions or owners, which fits the 'let's take this offline' behaviour. It does not test the claim that people call meetings so that no one decides alone. The Jabra figures are reported through press coverage, not from the original report.
sources.excerpt: 90% of Indian employees experience some level of meeting dread. | Indian workers average 8.8 hours in meetings weekly. | 58% of meeting time is perceived as unnecessary. | 66% of employees leave meetings without clear action items. | 59% require follow-up meetings to clarify decisions.

cover.headline: Eleven people on a meeting invite isn't a discussion. It's [insurance].
cover.sub: Every extra name on the invite is doing a job.

paragraphs: Eleven people on a meeting invite isn't a discussion. It's insurance.
The invite says "Quick sync", has no agenda and lists half the floor, plus two people from a team you've never met.
Everyone accepts. Declining feels riskier than sitting through it.
slides.why_swipe: So what happens inside the call?

paragraphs: So eleven people join. Three talk. The rest sit on mute with cameras off.
It ends with "Let's take this offline." Translation: decide it later, with fewer people watching.
slides.why_swipe: Why call eleven people to decide nothing?

paragraphs: Because deciding was never the point. The meeting exists so nobody has to decide alone.
If the plan flops, eleven people "aligned". Blame split eleven ways is no blame.
slides.why_swipe: Why would the organiser want that?

paragraphs: Look at it from the organiser's chair. A wrong call has one name on it. A slow call has none, it just eats everyone's Tuesday.
I've sent invites like that myself. Slow always felt safer.
And slow costs you. You go from one sync to the next.
By evening your calendar is full and your actual work hasn't started.
slides.why_swipe: So how do you read the next invite?

paragraphs: So skip the agenda and count the names.
Eleven people on the invite means one organiser who is scared to decide alone.

end.save: Read it again when the next "Quick sync" lands with half the floor on it.
end.send: Send to the colleague with back-to-back meetings and nothing done by evening.

draft.alt_text: An eight-slide text post arguing that big office meetings with many attendees and no agenda exist to spread blame, not to make decisions. It describes a 'Quick sync' invite with half the floor on it, where everyone accepts, three people talk, the rest stay on mute, and the call ends with 'let's take this offline', meaning decide later with fewer people watching. It explains that the meeting exists so nobody has to decide alone: a wrong call has one name on it, while a slow call has none and just eats everyone's time. The writer admits he has sent invites like that himself. Slow meetings leave your calendar full and your real work unstarted. It ends by saying you can skip the agenda and count the names: eleven people on the invite means one organiser who is scared to decide alone.
